To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the effect of fiscal shocks on the interest rate spread depends on the type of borrowing, (ii) the effect of a fiscal shock on the interest rate spreads depends on the identity of the agents who trigger default and/or inflation, (iii) the effect of default and inflation are not equivalent, and (iv) the effect of the fiscal shock on default depends on whether the government can borrow in domestic or foreign currency.

the distinction between domestic and foreign-currency debt matters, because the identity of the trigger of a debt crisis depends on the heterogeneously informed agent who makes the last decision, and that domestic-currency debt can be welfare-improving in a crisis, if the economy is not too small and the fiscal shock is large enough.

the choice between domestic- and foreign-currency denominated borrowing is determined by the identity of agents who are most likely to be uninformed, and that domestic-currency borrowing is more resilient to fiscal shock.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, if the government can credibly commit to not inflate, it should not default, and if it cannot credibly commit to no inflation, it should default.
the role of inflation in debt crises is not as straightforward as it might appear at first.

the role of information in debt crises is to break the equivalence between inflation and default, and thus the role of information is to distinguish between domestic and foreign-currency denominated debt.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the choice between inflation and default is determined by the relative strength of the domestic bondholder and the domestic laborer.
, in a frictionless world, inflation and default have the same economic impact, but in an imperfect world, the distinction matters.
, if a country is able to borrow in a foreign currency, then domestic inflation is a better way of defaulting than defaulting on the debt.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when heterogeneity in beliefs is present, the choice of currency in which to borrow matters for the resilience of an economy to fiscal shocks.
the role of inflation in debt crises is determined by the information structure of the economy.
the distinction between domestic-currency and foreign-currency debt is crucial in understanding how fiscal shocks are transmitted into crises.
